content.text: Velocity-time graphs show how velocity changes over time. Unlike distance-time graphs, they can show direction (positive and negative velocities) and allow us to calculate both acceleration and displacement directly from the graph.
Velocity-time graphs give you two key pieces of information: the gradient tells you the acceleration, and the area under the graph tells you the displacement (distance travelled).
The graph shows how velocity changes over time:
Above the x-axis: moving in the positive direction
Below the x-axis: moving in the negative direction

Area above the x-axis: positive displacement (moving forward)
Area below the x-axis: negative displacement (moving backward)
Total displacement = positive area - negative area
To calculate the area under a velocity-time graph, break the shape into rectangles and triangles. Area of a triangle = 1/2 x base x height. Area of a rectangle = base x height.

ECU (Engine Control Unit) data from cars can be plotted to analyse driving patterns.
Athletes' velocity profiles help coaches optimise performance.
Black box data from vehicles provides velocity-time information for crash analysis.
Engineers use velocity-time graphs to design safe and thrilling rides.

Do not confuse velocity-time graphs with distance-time graphs. On a v-t graph, a horizontal line means constant velocity (not stationary), and the area under the graph gives distance, not the y-value.
"A line going down means moving backward"
— A line going down means decelerating (slowing down). Only when the line crosses below zero does the object move backward.
— On a velocity-time graph, gradient gives acceleration, not speed. Speed is read directly from the y-axis.
— Area gives displacement. Distance requires taking absolute values of areas above and below the axis.
— A horizontal line means constant velocity. The object is only stationary if the horizontal line is on the x-axis (v = 0).
— Negative velocity means moving in the negative direction. The object could be speeding up, slowing down, or at constant speed.
